paras: The reported lynching of Abe Twiggs was the killing, according to an Augusta wire dispatch, of a Black man in Burke County, Georgia, on the night of Thursday, January 27, 1881, by lynchers believed to be Black. Twiggs had testified against his two brothers in a murder trial, and the dispatch tied his death to anger over that testimony. The story ran in brief across the country, but three days after it appeared the Savannah Morning News called it a false report and said Twiggs had been seen alive.

On November 27, 1880, William Driscoll, an overseer described as an Irishman, on the Miller estate in Burke County, was killed, and two Black laborers, Mose and Frank Twiggs, were arrested and convicted of his murder in Burke County Superior Court that December. Their brother Abe turned State's evidence and was the principal witness against them, and the Alexandria Gazette's version of the wire said that "this betrayal of his brothers caused great indignation among the colored people." Mose Twiggs was hanged in the jail yard at Waynesboro while several hundred Black residents gathered outside, after confessing that he alone had done the killing; Frank was reprieved for three weeks.

A dispatch dated Augusta, January 31, stated that Abe Twiggs, "colored," had been lynched in Burke County on Thursday night and that "it is supposed that he was lynched by negroes." A fuller version dated February 1 said only that "news has reached" Augusta of the killing, and described Twiggs as "taken out and lynched, his body being riddled with bullets." A later ready-print version added that he had been visiting relatives when he was taken out of the house, though no account says where he was shot. No report gives the number of attackers, names any of them, or describes a body or an inquest.

On February 4 the Savannah Morning News reported that the story circulated in Augusta "last Tuesday" had "turned out to be a false report, as Twiggs has been seen alive since the reported lynching." No arrests were reported, and later in February a brief noted that Frank Twiggs had also been executed at Waynesboro for the Driscoll murder.

The dispatch reached western and eastern dailies on February 1 and 2 under headings such as "Lynching in Georgia," "A Witness Lynched" and "A Negro Lynched." Most versions were one or two sentences that presented Black lynchers as a supposition, and one news summary renamed the victim "Abraham Twiggs." Between February 9 and 11 the item moved into the crime and news-summary columns of weekly papers, among them the Warren Sheaf, the Bismarck Tribune and the Gloucester County Democrat. A ready-print version carried by the Batesville Guard, the Iron County Register and the Iola Register garbled Burke County as "Burrell County." The Watertown Republican placed the lynching at Augusta "on the 31st ult," confusing the dispatch's dateline with the event, and attributed it to "a mob."

The only Georgia paper in the coverage treated the matter differently, dismissing it in a short state-news paragraph as a false report. None of the papers that had printed the lynching is shown carrying that correction, and the weekly reprints continued for a week after the denial.

Whether Twiggs was killed at all is disputed: the wire report, which its own Augusta correspondent framed as news that had "reached here," says he was shot to death, while the Savannah Morning News says he was alive. The Savannah denial came from a Georgia paper and was later, but it named no source, and no local Burke County or Augusta report appears in the coverage to settle the question.

reader.title: Reported lynching of Abe Twiggs
bases: Wire reports described Abe Twiggs as taken out at night and shot to death by supposed Black lynchers in retaliation for his testimony [A3, A13], though a Georgia paper called the report false [A8].

The wire said Twiggs was 'taken out and lynched' by unnamed 'lynchers' as punishment for testifying against his brothers [A3, A13], but the Savannah Morning News reported that he had been seen alive and the report was false [A8], so whether anyone was killed is unresolved; the group's size is never given.

All lynching reports trace to one Augusta dispatch that itself relayed hearsay ('News has reached here') [A3, A6], and the Savannah Morning News, a Georgia paper writing three days later, called it a false report [A8].

accounts.label: Augusta wire dispatch
accounts.gist: News 'reached' Augusta that Abe Twiggs was taken out Thursday night and lynched, his body riddled with bullets, by lynchers 'supposed to be negroes' angered by his testimony against his brothers.

accounts.label: Later ready-print version
accounts.gist: Adds that he was visiting relatives when he was taken out of the house and lynched.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News (Georgia)
accounts.gist: The report circulated in Augusta on Tuesday was false; Twiggs had been seen alive since the reported lynching.

framing.detail: Northern and western dailies ran the Augusta dispatch as a one- or two-sentence item under heads such as 'Lynching in Georgia' and 'A Negro Lynched', attributing it to Black lynchers on supposition.
The Alexandria Gazette's 'A Witness Lynched' framed it as punishment for 'This betrayal of his brothers' and the 'indignation among the colored people'.
Weekly ready-print columns folded it into lists of crimes ('Murderous Deeds'), some garbling the county as 'Burrell' or the place as Augusta.
The Savannah Morning News dismissed the story in its Georgia news column as a 'false report'.

conflicts.note: The wire account was hearsay relayed from Augusta and every later version repeats it; the denial comes from a Georgia paper three days later but names no source. Neither side is confirmed by an inquest or local report in the coverage.
The Jan. 31 date matches the Sacramento dispatch's dateline and is probably a garble.
Augusta is the dispatch dateline; 'Burrell' is a garble of Burke.
Background only; the Waynesboro dispatch to the Savannah paper says 'this morning' under a Jan. 28 dateline.
